cards.back: The combination of earned income, investment (portfolio) income, and passive income. Used to determine the investor's income tax rate. Short-term capital gains are also taxed as ordinary income.
Income derived from active participation in a trade or business — salary, wages, bonuses, tips, and consulting fees. Eligibility for IRA contributions is based ONLY on earned income.
Income earned from one's investments, including dividends and interest payments. Short-term capital gains are also added to ordinary income.

Investment income derived from direct participation programs (DPPs) such as limited partnerships and many real estate investments. Passive losses may ONLY be used to offset passive income — not earned or portfolio income.

cards.front: What is the holding period requirement for long-term capital gains treatment?
cards.back: The position must be held for MORE than one year. A holding period of one year or less is short-term.

cards.front: How are short-term capital gains taxed compared to long-term capital gains?
cards.back: Short-term gains (held one year or less) are taxed as ordinary income. Long-term gains (held more than one year) are taxed at an advantaged (lower) rate.

cards.front: How may capital losses be used to reduce taxes?
cards.back: Capital losses offset capital gains dollar-for-dollar. Any excess losses may reduce ordinary income by up to $3,000 per year. Losses beyond that may be carried forward indefinitely with no time limit.

cards.front: An investor has $24,000 in capital gains and $32,000 in capital losses during the tax year. How are these treated for tax purposes?
cards.back: Net loss = $8,000. The investor may use $3,000 to reduce ordinary income this year, and carry forward the remaining $5,000 into future tax years indefinitely.

cards.front: A customer has $120,000 in ordinary income. They sold one position for a $47,000 gain and another for a $50,000 loss. What is the customer's tax exposure?
cards.back: The $47,000 gain is fully offset by $50,000 in losses, leaving a $3,000 net loss. The customer pays tax on $117,000 in ordinary income ($120,000 − $3,000) and zero net gains.

cards.front: Do unrealized gains and losses have tax consequences?
cards.back: No. Unrealized gains/losses occur on open positions and have no tax impact. Tax consequences are triggered only when the position is closed and the gain/loss becomes realized.
If an investor sells a security at a loss and purchases the same or a substantially identical security within 30 days before OR after the sale, the loss is disallowed for tax purposes.
No — the wash sale itself is not illegal. What is illegal (or rather disallowed) is attempting to claim the loss from the wash sale to reduce taxes. The IRS simply disallows the loss.

cards.front: What securities are considered 'substantially identical' under the wash sale rule?
cards.back: Any security that can be converted or exercised into the security sold at a loss — including call options, rights, warrants, convertible bonds, and convertible preferred stock from the same issuer. The rule also applies to recreating short positions.

cards.front: On June 1, an investor sells XYZ stock at a loss. On June 20, the investor buys XYZ call options. Is the loss allowed?
cards.back: No. The call options are considered substantially identical to XYZ stock because they can be exercised to acquire XYZ shares. The purchase within 30 days triggers the wash sale rule and the loss is disallowed.

cards.front: Selma purchased Ohm Electric stock on July 10 for $18/share and sold it on June 10 the following year for $22/share. What kind of gain or loss is this?
cards.back: Short-term capital gain. The holding period (July 10 to June 10) is 11 months — one year or less — so it does not qualify for long-term treatment. The $4/share profit is taxed as ordinary income.

cards.front: Which of the following is NOT taxed as ordinary income: an employer bonus, bond interest payments, profit from a long-held security sale, or consulting fees?
cards.back: Profit from the sale of a long-held (more than one year) security — it is a long-term capital gain taxed at an advantaged rate. Bonuses and consulting fees are earned income; bond interest is portfolio income; both are ordinary income.

cards.front: Can passive losses be used to offset earned income or portfolio income?
cards.back: No. Passive losses may ONLY be used to offset passive income. They cannot offset earned income, dividends, interest, or capital gains.
